Breast Cancer
By: Julianna Ingrassia, Tina Lin, Kalev Pineles, Mackenzie Shuey, 
Robbie Fiedorek, Kalliopi Gaidatzis, Mia Gyorfi, Giovanna Scimone 
NURS 4210: NURSING PRAC ADULT CLIENT III

Risk Factors and Prevention
Risk Factors
Non-Modifiable
● Female gender at birth
● Age: the risk increases with age especially after age 50
● Family history of breast cancer
● Early menarche before age 12 or late menopause after 
age 55
● Dense breast tissue 
Modifiable
● Obesity 
● Lack of physical activity
● Alcohol consumption and tobacco use 
● Long-term hormone therapy
● Nulliparity or pregnancy after age 30 
● Lack of breastfeeding 
Prevention
● Maintain healthy weight and exercising 
● Limiting alcohol consumption 
● Avoid long-term hormone therapy
● Breastfeeding 
● Genetic counseling and testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 
as well as HER2
● Preventive medication for those at high risk

Health Promotion and Early Detection
Health Promotion 
● Teach patient how to perform breast self-exams and 
report any changes to their doctors 
● Encourage patient to get regular checkups and to 
communicate openly with their healthcare providers
● Encourage participation in community events that 
promote breast cancer screening such as Breast 
Cancer Awareness Month
● Reduce barriers to screening, such as low health 
literacy, financial barriers, and cultural or personal 
beliefs 
Early Detection
● Monthly breast self-exams to become familiar 
with how one’s breasts normally look and feel
● Clinical breast exams by a healthcare provider
● Mammogram done every year from age 40 (per 
American College of Radiology and Society of 
Breast Imaging guidelines; breastcancer.orgs)
● Patients at high risk should undergo screening 
mammography at an earlier age and more 
frequently as recommended by their healthcare 
provider 
● Screening decisions should align with present 
surgical history, and duration of gender-affirming 
hormone therapy, regardless of outward gender 
presentation or legal sex designation
Warning Signs to Teach Patients
● Lump or thickening of breast tissue
● Nipple retraction or skin dimpling 
● Nipple discharge 
● Swelling of one breast or uneven size or shape

Diagnostic Tests — Nursing Responsibilities in Breast Cancer Workup
1. Mammography & Clinical Breast Exam
Looks for: Masses, calcifications, or asymmetry in breast tissue.
Nursing Implications: Avoid deodorant/lotion/powder day of exam. Schedule post-menses if 
possible to reduce tenderness. Reassure her through the brief compression discomfort.
2. Breast Ultrasound
Looks for: Cystic vs. solid mass; a follow-up tool, not a first-line screen.
Nursing Implications: Painless, no prep needed. Also used to guide biopsy needle placement.
3. Breast MRI
Looks for: Extent of disease or additional tumors, often for high-risk patients.
Nursing Implications: Screen for pacemakers, metal implants, or claustrophobia. Check renal 
function and contrast allergies; start IV access.
4. Biopsy
Looks for: Definitive diagnosis; whether the mass is cancerous.
Nursing Implications: Confirm consent and NPO status if sedated. Post-procedure: watch for 
bleeding/infection, ice the site, teach warning signs.
5. Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy
Looks for: Spread to nearby lymph nodes; key for staging.
Nursing Implications: Warn her tracer/dye may tint urine or skin. Monitor injection site; assess 
arm for early lymphedema postop.
6. Genetic Testing
Looks for: Hormone/HER2 status (guides therapy) and inherited mutation risk (BRCA).
Nursing Implications: Explain what results mean for treatment. Provide genetic counseling and 
emotional support; protect confidentiality.

Medical Management
Treatment depends on the type, stage, and receptor status of the cancer.
● Surgery
○ Lumpectomy: surgery that removes a breast lump or tumor while keeping most of the 
breast intact
○ Mastectomy: surgery that removes the entire breast
○ Lymph node removal: surgery that removes the lymph nodes 
● Radiation therapy may be used after surgery to destroy remaining cancer cells.
● Chemotherapy may be given before or after surgery to kill cancer cells.
● Hormone therapy for hormone receptor–positive cancers:
○ Tamoxifen
○ Aromatase inhibitors
○ Fulvestrant
● Targeted therapy for cancers with specific biomarkers:
○ Trastuzumab
○ Pertuzumab
● Immunotherapy may be used for certain breast cancers, particularly some triple-negative 
cancers.
Treatment may involve a combination of surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, 
targeted therapy, and/or immunotherapy.

Medication Management & Nursing Responsibilities
Chemotherapy
● Antineoplastic agents disrupt 
growth of cancer cells and 
reduce recurrence risk
● Common drugs: doxorubicin, 
cyclophosphamide, 
paclitaxel
Nursing Responsibilities
● Monitor CBC, renal/hepatic 
function, and signs of 
infection
● Assess for neutropenia, 
anemia, thrombocytopenia, 
nausea/vomiting, and 
peripheral neuropathy
● Teach infection precautions
Hormonal Therapy
● For estrogen or progesterone 
receptor-positive cancer
● Selective estrogen receptor 
modulators (SERMs) - tamoxifen, 
toremifene
● Selective estrogen receptor 
degraders (SERDs) - fulvestrant
● Aromatase inhibitors - anastrozole, 
letrozole
Nursing Responsibilities
● For antiestrogens
○ Monitor for thromboembolism and 
abnormal vaginal bleeding
○ Teach patient to report leg 
swelling/pain, chest pain, dyspnea
● For aromatase inhibitors
○ Monitor for bone loss, fractures, 
arthralgia
○ Encourage weight-bearing 
exercise and adequate calcium/vit 
D
Targeted Therapy
● For HER2-positive cancer, 
monoclonal antibodies block 
HER2 activity
● Trastuzumab (Herceptin), 
pertuzumab (Perjeta)
Nursing Responsibilities
● Monitor cardiac function, 
especially ejection fraction, 
before and during treatment
● Monitor for infusion reactions

Patient & Family Education
ASSESS & PERSONALIZE
• Assess understanding, preferred language, and 
support needs.
• Reinforce how stage and ER/PR/HER2 results 
relate to the prescribed plan.
• Discuss fertility referral before treatment, if 
relevant.
SUPPORT & EVALUATE
• With permission, include a chosen support 
person; address emotional, body image, and 
practical needs.
• Use teach-back: ask the patient to explain the 
plan, urgent symptoms, and whom to call. Reteach 
gaps.
TREATMENT SAFETY
• Review expected side effects and prescribed 
symptom relief; teach hand hygiene during 
chemotherapy.
• During chemotherapy, fever ≥100.4°F 
(38°C): call the oncology team 
immediately.
• Give daytime and after-hours contact numbers.
Sources: National Cancer Institute; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Discharge Planning & Homecare
● Incision & drain care:Keep the 
surgical area clean and dry as 
instructed; teach the patient how to 
empty and record output from a JP 
drain if present.
● Pain management:Take 
prescribed pain medications as 
directed and report pain that is 
worsening or not controlled.
● Activity: Gradually return to 
normal activity and follow 
lifting/exercise restrictions. Perform 
prescribed arm and shoulder 
exercises to maintain range of 
motion and prevent stiffness.
● Monitor for complications:
Report fever, redness, warmth, 
increased swelling, worsening 
pain, or drainage from the incision. 
Seek immediate care for difficulty 
breathing.
● Lymphedema awareness:Teach 
the patient to monitor the affected 
arm/chest for new swelling, 
tightness, or pain, especially if 
lymph nodes were removed.
● Follow-up care: Reinforce 
scheduled surgical/oncology 
follow-ups and continued treatment 
or screening as ordered.

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 1
A client is 10 days into her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer and calls the clinic saying she 
feels "a little warm." Her temperature at home read 100.6 °F. What is the nurse’s best response?
A.  Take acetaminophen and recheck her temperature in a few hours
B.  Increase fluids and rest, and call back if it goes above 101°F
C.  Go to the ED right away — this needs to be addressed immediately
D.  This is a normal side effect of chemo and doesn’t need to be reported

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 1 — ANSWER
A.  Take acetaminophen and recheck her temperature in a few hours
B.  Increase fluids and rest, and call back if it goes above 101°F
C.  Go to the ED right away — this needs to be addressed immediately
D.  This is a normal side effect of chemo and doesn’t need to be reported
Rationale: Any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher during chemotherapy has to be treated as a possible sign of neutropenic sepsis 
and evaluated right away. Chemo may suppress the immune response without the client appearing or feeling very sick.

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 2
A client is three weeks post-op from an axillary lymph node dissection and reports new swelling in her affected arm, which 
she’s also been using for home blood pressure checks. What’s the priority teaching here?
A.  She should avoid blood pressure checks, injections, or blood draws on that arm from now on, and this new swelling needs 
to be looked into
B.  Some swelling this soon after surgery is expected and should clear up on its own
C.  She should wrap the arm snugly with an ace bandage to bring the swelling down
D.  This probably isn’t related to the surgery — she can just mention it to her primary doctor at some point

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 2 — ANSWER
A.  She should avoid blood pressure checks, injections, or blood draws on that arm from now on, and this 
new swelling needs to be looked into
B.  Some swelling this soon after surgery is expected and should clear up on its own
C.  She should wrap the arm snugly with an ace bandage to bring the swelling down
D. This probably isn’t related to the surgery — she can just mention it to her primary doctor at some point
Rationale: Removing lymph nodes affects normal lymph drainage, so that arm needs lifelong protection from anything that adds 
pressure or constriction, and new swelling has to be reported since it could indicate the development of  lymphedema.
